prompt: If I _____ harder at school, I would have a better job now.
why: Mixed conditional: past condition (had + pp) → present result (would + inf).

prompt: She _____ healthier now if she hadn't started smoking.
why: Past cause → present result uses 'would + inf' in the result clause.

prompt: If they _____ the map, they wouldn't be lost right now.
why: Past condition (had + pp) explains a present state.

prompt: He _____ more confident if he had practised public speaking.
why: 'Would be' signals a present result of a past unfulfilled condition.

prompt: If I _____ a degree, I could apply for this position today.
why: 'Had had' = past perfect for a past unfulfilled condition with present consequence.

prompt: If he _____ (take) that job offer, he would be living abroad now.
why: Past unfulfilled condition requires past perfect.

prompt: She _____ (not/be) so stressed today if she had slept properly last night.
why: Present result of past failure → 'wouldn't be'.

prompt: If they _____ (invest) early, they would own a house by now.
why: Past perfect in the if-clause for a past missed opportunity.

prompt: I _____ (know) the answer right now if I had studied the chapter.
why: 'Would know' in the result clause for present consequence.

prompt: If she _____ (choose) medicine, she would be a doctor today.
why: Past perfect condition → present result.

prompt: Combine: 'He didn't save money. He can't retire now.'
answer: If he had saved money, he could retire now.
accept: If he had saved money, he could retire now.
He could retire now if he had saved money.
why: Mixed conditional links past action to present ability.

prompt: Combine: 'She didn't learn to drive. She can't take the job.'
answer: If she had learned to drive, she could take the job.
accept: If she had learned to drive, she could take the job.
She could take the job if she had learned to drive.
why: Past condition → present modal result.

prompt: Write a mixed conditional sentence about a past decision that affects your life today.
model_answer: If I had studied Spanish at school, I would be able to travel more easily in South America now.

prompt: Write a mixed conditional sentence about a skill you wish you had developed earlier.
model_answer: If I had practised piano as a child, I could play it professionally now.

prompt: _____ had she left the building when the fire alarm sounded.
why: 'Hardly had + subject + pp' triggers inversion; 'No sooner' also works but needs 'than', not 'when'.

prompt: Not only _____ he rude to the staff, but he also refused to pay.
why: 'Not only was he…' — inversion after negative adverbials uses auxiliary before subject.

prompt: Never before _____ I seen such a beautiful sunset.
why: 'Never before had I…' — past perfect inversion for dramatic effect.

prompt: _____ would I accept such unfair terms.
why: 'Under no circumstances would I…' — full inversion with 'would'.

prompt: No sooner had the concert begun _____ it started to rain.
why: 'No sooner…than' is the fixed collocation.

prompt: Seldom _____ (see) I such poor customer service before.
why: 'Seldom' triggers inversion: auxiliary + subject + pp.

prompt: Not until she apologised _____ (agree) he to continue the meeting.
why: 'Not until…did he agree' — past simple inversion.

prompt: Only when the results came in _____ (realise) they how serious it was.
why: 'Only when…did they realise' — inversion in main clause.

prompt: Barely _____ (sit) she down before the phone rang.
why: 'Barely had she sat' — past perfect inversion.

prompt: Little _____ (know) he that his plan would backfire.
why: 'Little did he know' — fixed inverted expression.

prompt: Rewrite with inversion: 'I had never heard such a powerful speech.'
answer: Never had I heard such a powerful speech.
accept: Never had I heard such a powerful speech.
why: 'Never' fronted → past perfect inversion.

prompt: Rewrite with inversion: 'She not only failed the exam but also lost her scholarship.'
answer: Not only did she fail the exam, but she also lost her scholarship.
accept: Not only did she fail the exam, but she also lost her scholarship.
Not only did she fail the exam but she also lost her scholarship.
why: 'Not only did she fail…' — inversion in first clause only.

prompt: Write a sentence using 'Rarely' or 'Seldom' with correct subject-auxiliary inversion.
model_answer: Rarely does the manager attend the morning briefing herself.

prompt: Write a dramatic sentence about a surprising event using 'No sooner…than'.
rubric: Simple past or similar in second clause
model_answer: No sooner had we arrived at the airport than the flight was cancelled.

prompt: The suspect is believed _____ the country before the arrest.
why: Passive reporting verb + perfect infinitive for a prior action.

prompt: It _____ that the economy will improve next year.
why: Impersonal passive: 'It is expected that…'

prompt: The documents are said _____ stolen from the archive.
why: 'To have been stolen' — passive perfect infinitive after reporting verb.

prompt: She _____ to have misled investors, according to the report.
why: 'Is alleged to have…' — impersonal passive reporting structure.

prompt: A new cure _____ by the research team by the end of the decade.
why: Future perfect passive for a completed future action.

prompt: The missing funds _____ (believe / steal) by a senior employee.
answer: are believed to have been stolen
accept: are believed to have been stolen
why: Present passive + perfect passive infinitive.

prompt: It _____ (report) that hundreds of people were left homeless.
why: Impersonal passive in present perfect.

prompt: The bridge _____ (repair) before winter arrives.
why: Future perfect passive.

prompt: He _____ (know) to be an expert in cybersecurity.
why: Simple present passive reporting.

prompt: The new policy _____ (implement) gradually over the next six months.
why: Future simple passive.

prompt: Make passive: 'Experts believe that the painting was forged in the 1980s.'
answer: The painting is believed to have been forged in the 1980s.
accept: The painting is believed to have been forged in the 1980s.
It is believed that the painting was forged in the 1980s.
why: Two passive patterns for reporting verbs.

prompt: Make passive: 'They will have completed the survey by Friday.'
answer: The survey will have been completed by Friday.
accept: The survey will have been completed by Friday.
why: Future perfect passive: 'will have been + pp'.

prompt: Write a sentence using the impersonal passive ('It is said/believed/reported…') about a current news topic.
rubric: Uses impersonal 'It is + reporting verb + that'
model_answer: It is widely believed that renewable energy will replace fossil fuels within the next thirty years.

prompt: Write a sentence using a personal passive reporting structure ('She is thought to have…').
rubric: Subject + passive reporting verb + perfect infinitive
model_answer: The CEO is thought to have known about the data breach weeks before it was made public.

prompt: The committee recommended that the report _____ revised immediately.
why: Mandative subjunctive after 'recommend that': bare infinitive form.

prompt: It is essential that every candidate _____ the form in full.
why: Subjunctive after 'it is essential that': no -s ending even in third person.

prompt: If I _____ you, I would speak to the manager directly.
why: 'If I were you' — mandative subjunctive / hypothetical 'were' for all persons.

prompt: She insists that he _____ present at the hearing.
why: 'Insist that' triggers mandative subjunctive: bare 'be'.

prompt: It is vital that the data _____ encrypted before transmission.
why: Subjunctive 'be' after 'it is vital that'.

prompt: The judge ordered that the evidence _____ (present) to the jury immediately.
why: Passive subjunctive after 'ordered that'.

prompt: We suggest that she _____ (apply) for the scholarship before the deadline.
why: Bare infinitive subjunctive after 'suggest that'.

prompt: It is important that he _____ (not/miss) any of the sessions.
why: Negative subjunctive: 'not + bare infinitive', no auxiliary.

prompt: They demanded that the CEO _____ (resign) at once.
why: Mandative subjunctive after 'demand that'.

prompt: If he _____ (be) more experienced, he would handle the situation differently.
why: Hypothetical 'were' for all persons in present/future conditionals.

prompt: Rewrite using mandative subjunctive: 'The doctor said he must rest.'
answer: The doctor recommended that he rest.
accept: The doctor recommended that he rest.
The doctor insisted that he rest.
The doctor suggested that he rest.
why: 'Must' replaced by reporting verb + subjunctive.

prompt: Rewrite: 'It is important for everyone to attend.'
answer: It is important that everyone attend.
accept: It is important that everyone attend.
why: 'For + infinitive' → 'that + subjunctive'.

prompt: Write a sentence using the mandative subjunctive after a verb of requirement (demand, insist, require, propose).
model_answer: The board proposed that the annual budget be reviewed by an independent auditor.

prompt: Write a 'wish' or 'if only' sentence using the subjunctive to express a present regret.
rubric: Uses 'wish/if only + past tense or were'
model_answer: I wish I were more confident when speaking in public.

prompt: _____ John who broke the window, not Mary.
why: Cleft sentence: 'It was + focus + who/that' for emphasis.

prompt: What she needs _____ a good night's sleep.
why: Pseudo-cleft: 'What she needs is…' — singular verb agrees with complement.

prompt: It was the new manager _____ introduced the flexible working policy.
why: 'Who' for a person in a cleft, though 'that' is also acceptable.

prompt: What surprised me most _____ the low turnout.
why: Pseudo-cleft verb agrees with the complement noun.

prompt: It is not money _____ he is after; it is recognition.
why: 'That' is standard in cleft sentences for things; 'which' is also used in formal writing.

prompt: _____ I really enjoy about this city is the diversity of the food scene.
why: Pseudo-cleft opens with 'What' when the focus is the subject complement.

prompt: It was in 1969 _____ humans first walked on the Moon.
why: Cleft with time adverbial uses 'that'.

prompt: What the company needs to do is _____ its pricing strategy.
why: After 'is' in a pseudo-cleft, bare or 'to-' infinitive is accepted.

prompt: It _____ the accountant who noticed the discrepancy in the figures.
why: 'It was' is the standard past cleft opener.

prompt: What bothers me _____ the constant background noise in the office.
why: Singular complement → singular 'is'.

prompt: Rewrite with a cleft to emphasise 'the director': 'The director approved the budget.'
answer: It was the director who approved the budget.
accept: It was the director who approved the budget.
It was the director that approved the budget.
why: 'It was + focus noun + who/that'.

prompt: Rewrite as a pseudo-cleft: 'I most admire her dedication.'
answer: What I most admire is her dedication.
accept: What I most admire is her dedication.
What I admire most is her dedication.
why: 'What + subject + verb + is + focus'.

prompt: Write a cleft sentence to emphasise when or where something important happened.
model_answer: It was in this very building that the peace treaty was signed in 1945.

prompt: Write a pseudo-cleft sentence starting with 'What' to describe something you value about learning languages.
model_answer: What I value most about learning languages is the ability to connect with people from different cultures.

prompt: The project was underfunded. _____, the team delivered on time.
why: 'However' signals contrast between two statements.

prompt: Sales rose sharply in Q3. _____, the company decided to expand.
why: 'Consequently' signals a result.

prompt: She is talented. _____, she lacks the necessary experience.
why: 'That said' acknowledges a concession before introducing a contrast.

prompt: The report was well written. _____, it contained several factual errors.
why: 'Nonetheless' = despite the positive, a negative follows.

prompt: The policy is unpopular. _____, the government plans to proceed.
why: 'Even so' = despite opposition, the action continues.

prompt: The new law is controversial. _____, supporters argue it will reduce inequality.
why: Concessive marker before a counter-argument.

prompt: The presentation was unclear. _____, attendees left confused.
why: Cause-effect marker.

prompt: He is an expert in finance. _____, he has little knowledge of marketing.
why: Contrast marker.

prompt: The product is expensive. _____, it offers excellent value for money.
why: Concessive pivot.

prompt: Staff turnover has increased. _____, morale is at an all-time low.
why: Addition marker piling on related negative points.

prompt: Connect with a suitable discourse marker: 'The weather was terrible. We enjoyed the trip.'
answer: The weather was terrible. Nevertheless, we enjoyed the trip.
accept: The weather was terrible. Nevertheless, we enjoyed the trip.
The weather was terrible. However, we enjoyed the trip.
The weather was terrible. Even so, we enjoyed the trip.
Although the weather was terrible, we enjoyed the trip.
why: Concessive linkage between contrasting ideas.

prompt: Connect with a result marker: 'The heating broke. The office was closed.'
answer: The heating broke. As a result, the office was closed.
accept: The heating broke. As a result, the office was closed.
The heating broke. Consequently, the office was closed.
The heating broke, so the office was closed.
why: Result/cause-effect discourse marker.

prompt: Write a short 3-sentence paragraph about a decision, using at least two different discourse markers (contrast, addition, or result).
rubric: Two distinct discourse markers used correctly
model_answer: The company decided to launch the product in spring. Moreover, it planned a major advertising campaign. However, unexpected supply issues delayed the release by three months.

prompt: Write a concession sentence using 'Despite' or 'In spite of' followed by a noun phrase.
rubric: 'Despite/In spite of' followed by a noun phrase (not 'that')
Main clause expresses a contrasting outcome
model_answer: Despite the heavy rain, the outdoor ceremony went ahead as planned.

prompt: The results _____ suggest a correlation between stress and productivity.
why: 'May' hedges the claim appropriately; all options hedge but 'may' is simplest modal hedge here.

prompt: It _____ that further research is needed to confirm these findings.
why: 'It would seem' is a common hedging structure.

prompt: The data _____ indicate a downward trend in consumer confidence.
why: 'Appear to' hedges without being redundant like 'could possibly'.

prompt: _____ the most significant factor is the lack of investment.
why: 'Arguably' signals the writer's tentative opinion; 'allegedly' implies unproven accusation.

prompt: There _____ be a link between diet and mental health, although evidence is mixed.
why: 'Could' expresses possibility with epistemic caution.

prompt: The evidence _____ (suggest) that urban areas are warming faster than rural ones.
why: Hedged reporting of evidence.

prompt: It _____ (be) premature to draw firm conclusions at this stage.
why: Hedging an evaluation or judgement.

prompt: This _____ (explain) why absenteeism rates have risen so sharply.
why: Modal hedge before a content verb.

prompt: _____, the current approach is unsustainable in the long term.
why: Adverb hedge to signal the writer's opinion without stating it as fact.

prompt: There _____ (be) several reasons for the observed decline.
why: Hedged existential claim.

prompt: Make this less certain: 'Social media causes anxiety in teenagers.'
answer: Social media may cause anxiety in teenagers.
accept: Social media may cause anxiety in teenagers.
Social media appears to cause anxiety in teenagers.
There appears to be a link between social media and anxiety in teenagers.
It could be argued that social media causes anxiety in teenagers.
why: Add a modal or hedging phrase to soften the claim.

prompt: Rewrite in academic hedged style: 'This proves our theory is correct.'
answer: This would appear to support our theory.
accept: This would appear to support our theory.
This seems to support our theory.
This could be seen as evidence for our theory.
why: Replace 'proves' + 'correct' with hedged equivalents.

prompt: Write one hedged sentence presenting a possible cause for a social trend (e.g., rising obesity, declining birth rates).
rubric: Uses at least one hedging device (modal, 'appear to', 'arguably', etc.)
Does not state speculation as fact
model_answer: One factor that may contribute to declining birth rates is the rising cost of housing, which arguably makes family planning more challenging for younger generations.

prompt: Write an academic sentence conceding a counterargument using 'While it is true that…, it could be argued that…'
rubric: Uses concession structure 'While it is true that…'
model_answer: While it is true that technology has created new jobs, it could be argued that the pace of automation poses a significant threat to employment in the manufacturing sector.

prompt: Choose the nominalised version: 'The government decided to reduce taxes.'
options: The government's decision to reduce taxes
The government deciding to reduce taxes
The government had decided about taxes
why: 'The government's decision to reduce taxes' turns the verb into a noun phrase.

prompt: Which sentence uses nominalisation?
options: The rapid approval of the plan came as a surprise.
why: 'The rapid approval' nominalises the verb 'approved'.

prompt: The verb 'analyse' → nominalised form:
why: 'Analysis' is the noun form of 'analyse'.

prompt: 'Develop' → most appropriate nominalisation in formal writing:
why: 'Development' is the standard nominalisation.

prompt: Nominalise: 'The team failed to meet the deadline.'
options: The team's failure to meet the deadline
The team was failing the deadline
The team not meeting the deadline
why: 'The team's failure to meet the deadline' — possessive + nominalisation.

prompt: The _____ (investigate) into the accident took three months.
why: 'Investigation' nominalises 'investigate'.

prompt: Her _____ (refuse) to cooperate surprised everyone.
why: 'Refusal' nominalises 'refuse'.

prompt: The sudden _____ (collapse) of the market wiped out savings.
why: 'Collapse' is already a noun; used directly as nominalisation.

prompt: The _____ (implement) of the new system will take six weeks.
why: 'Implementation' nominalises 'implement'.

prompt: There was widespread _____ (oppose) to the proposed changes.
why: 'Opposition' nominalises 'oppose'.

prompt: Nominalise: 'Scientists discovered a new compound.'
answer: The discovery of a new compound by scientists
accept: The discovery of a new compound by scientists
The scientists' discovery of a new compound
why: 'Discovery' replaces 'discovered'; agent moved to prepositional phrase.

prompt: Nominalise: 'They will implement the policy next year.'
answer: The implementation of the policy next year
accept: The implementation of the policy next year
why: 'Implementation' + 'of the policy'.

prompt: Rewrite a cause-effect sentence (e.g., 'Temperatures rose, which caused ice to melt') using nominalisations.
rubric: At least one verb converted to a noun
model_answer: The rise in temperatures led to the rapid melting of polar ice.

prompt: Write a formal sentence about a business or scientific topic using at least two nominalisations.
model_answer: The implementation of stricter regulations resulted in a significant reduction in carbon emissions.

prompt: 'I'll call you tomorrow,' she said. → She said she _____ call me the next day.
why: Back-shift: 'will' → 'would' in reported speech.

prompt: 'We have already submitted the report,' they said. → They said they _____ already submitted the report.
why: Present perfect → past perfect in reported speech.

prompt: He asked me _____ I had ever been to Japan.
why: Reported yes/no question uses 'if' or 'whether'.

prompt: She told me _____ the windows before leaving.
why: 'Tell someone to do something' — infinitive in reported command.

prompt: 'Don't touch anything!' the detective warned. → The detective warned us _____ anything.
why: Reported negative command: 'warned us not to touch'.

prompt: 'I'm feeling much better now,' he said. → He said he _____ (feel) much better then.
why: Present continuous → past continuous in reported speech.

prompt: She asked where _____ (live) before moving to London.
why: Past simple → past perfect in reported question.

prompt: 'You must submit the form by Friday,' he insisted. → He insisted that we _____ (submit) the form by Friday.
why: 'Must' → bare subjunctive or 'had to' in reported speech.

prompt: 'Can you help me?' she asked. → She asked if I _____ (can) help her.
why: 'Can' → 'could' in reported speech back-shift.

prompt: He recommended _____ (we / try) the fish restaurant on the corner.
why: 'Recommend + that + subjunctive' or 'recommend + -ing'.

prompt: Report: 'I didn't take the money,' the employee insisted.
answer: The employee insisted that he/she hadn't taken the money.
accept: The employee insisted that he hadn't taken the money.
The employee insisted that she hadn't taken the money.
The employee insisted they hadn't taken the money.
why: Past simple → past perfect; pronoun adjusted.

prompt: Report: 'Please be quiet during the performance,' the usher said.
answer: The usher asked us to be quiet during the performance.
accept: The usher asked us to be quiet during the performance.
The usher told us to be quiet during the performance.
why: Reported polite command: 'asked/told + us + to-infinitive'.

prompt: Report what a teacher or manager once said to you, using at least two different reporting verbs.
model_answer: My manager told me that the project was behind schedule and warned me not to miss any more deadlines. She also suggested that I delegate some tasks to other team members.

prompt: Write a short reported dialogue (2 turns) between two people using mixed reporting structures (statement + question).
rubric: At least one reported statement and one reported question
model_answer: She asked him whether he had finished the report yet. He replied that he had almost finished it but said he needed one more day to check the figures.

prompt: _____ tired she was, she stayed up to finish the assignment.
why: 'No matter how + adjective' concedes degree.

prompt: He passed the exam _____ studying very little.
why: 'Despite' + noun phrase (gerund).

prompt: _____ the fact that it was raining, the match continued.
why: 'Despite the fact that' or 'despite + noun phrase'.

prompt: She is fluent in three languages, _____ having never lived abroad.
why: 'Despite' + gerund phrase.

prompt: Much _____ I'd like to help, I simply don't have the time.
why: 'Much as I'd like to…' — concessive inversion with 'as'.

prompt: _____ all her efforts, she didn't manage to secure the contract.
why: 'Despite' before a noun phrase.

prompt: The café remains popular _____ its high prices.
why: Concession before a noun phrase.

prompt: _____ being exhausted, he agreed to work overtime.
why: 'Despite/In spite of' + gerund.

prompt: _____ the warnings, they went swimming in the rough sea.
why: Concession before plural noun.

prompt: Hard _____ it was to admit, she knew she had made a mistake.
why: Fronted adjective + 'as' = concessive inversion.

prompt: Combine with 'despite': 'She was very tired. She completed the marathon.'
answer: Despite being very tired, she completed the marathon.
accept: Despite being very tired, she completed the marathon.
She completed the marathon despite being very tired.
why: 'Despite' + gerund phrase; drop conjunction.

prompt: Rewrite using 'even though': 'In spite of the cold weather, they held the barbecue outside.'
answer: Even though the weather was cold, they held the barbecue outside.
accept: Even though the weather was cold, they held the barbecue outside.
They held the barbecue outside even though the weather was cold.
why: 'Even though' needs a full clause, not a noun phrase.

prompt: Write a sentence using 'despite' or 'in spite of' to describe something surprising about someone you admire.
rubric: 'Despite/In spite of' followed by noun phrase or gerund
Main clause expresses a contrasting or surprising result
model_answer: Despite having no formal training, she became one of the most respected architects of her generation.

prompt: Write a concessive sentence using 'no matter how' to show determination.
rubric: Main clause expresses resolve or outcome
model_answer: No matter how difficult the negotiations become, we are committed to finding a peaceful solution.

prompt: She _____ tell the truth — I witnessed it myself.
why: Emphatic 'did' in past tense to stress the truth of an assertion.

prompt: I know it seems unlikely, but he _____ exist.
why: 'Does' as emphatic present auxiliary before a main verb.

prompt: We _____ appreciate your support throughout this project.
why: 'Do appreciate' — present emphatic for expressing sincere gratitude.

prompt: If you _____ decide to apply, please submit your portfolio in advance.
why: Conditional emphatic 'do' stresses the action.

prompt: She _____ visit us last summer, despite what you heard.
why: 'Did visit' — past emphatic to contradict a previous statement.

prompt: I _____ (wish) you had told me sooner — it would have saved us a lot of time.
why: Emphatic 'do wish' in present for strong regret.

prompt: He _____ (try) hard; he just needs more support.
why: 'Does try' — emphatic third-person present.

prompt: They _____ (warn) us, but we didn't listen.
why: 'Did warn' — past emphatic to acknowledge a prior action.

prompt: Please _____ (come) to the ceremony if you can.
why: 'Do come' — emphatic imperative for warm invitation.

prompt: I _____ (believe) you; it's just a very unusual story.
why: Emphatic present 'do believe' to stress sincerity.

prompt: Add emphatic 'do/did' and rewrite: 'He studied hard for the exam.'
answer: He did study hard for the exam.
accept: He did study hard for the exam.
why: Insert 'did' before bare infinitive.

prompt: Make emphatic and rewrite: 'She knows how important this is.'
answer: She does know how important this is.
accept: She does know how important this is.
why: Insert 'does' before bare infinitive 'know'.

prompt: Write a sentence using emphatic 'do/does/did' to contradict a false assumption about yourself.
model_answer: I do enjoy socialising — I just prefer smaller gatherings to large parties.

prompt: Write an emphatic invitation or polite request using 'do + imperative'.
model_answer: Do let me know if there is anything I can do to help with the arrangements.

prompt: The hotel, _____ we stayed last summer, has now closed.
why: 'Where' replaces 'in which' for place in a non-defining relative clause.

prompt: The reason _____ she left is still unclear.
why: 'The reason why' — 'why' introduces a relative clause of reason.

prompt: That is the scientist _____ work changed our understanding of DNA.
why: 'Whose' shows possession in a relative clause.

prompt: The day _____ we first met was a public holiday.
why: 'When' for time references; 'on which' also correct but 'when' is simpler.

prompt: This is the company _____ I told you about.
why: 'That' preferred in defining relative clauses; 'which' also accepted.

prompt: The professor, _____ lectures I find fascinating, has just published a new book.
why: Possessive relative pronoun before a noun.

prompt: The moment _____ she realised her mistake was when she saw the results.
why: 'When' or 'that' for time reference in defining clause.

prompt: He is the colleague _____ I was telling you about.
why: 'Who/whom/that' for a person in defining relative clause.

prompt: The building, _____ construction took three years, is now a museum.
why: 'Whose' for inanimate nouns in non-defining clauses.

prompt: There are very few situations _____ this approach would not apply.
why: 'In which' / 'where' for location/context.

prompt: Combine: 'I met a scientist. Her research on climate change is groundbreaking.'
answer: I met a scientist whose research on climate change is groundbreaking.
accept: I met a scientist whose research on climate change is groundbreaking.
why: 'Whose' links possessor to the noun that follows.

prompt: Add a non-defining relative clause: 'The concert was sold out. It was held at the city hall.'
answer: The concert, which was held at the city hall, was sold out.
accept: The concert, which was held at the city hall, was sold out.
The concert, which was sold out, was held at the city hall.
why: Non-defining clause in commas with 'which' for things.

prompt: Write a sentence with a non-defining relative clause ('which' or 'who') giving extra information about a place or person.
model_answer: The library, which was built in the nineteenth century, holds one of the largest collections of rare manuscripts in the country.

prompt: Write a sentence using 'whose' in a relative clause about someone in your field of work or study.
model_answer: She works alongside a researcher whose findings on neuroplasticity have attracted international attention.

prompt: I wish I _____ more time to travel when I was younger.
why: 'Wish + past perfect' for regrets about the past.

prompt: If only she _____ harder, she might have passed.
why: 'If only + past perfect' expresses regret about a past action.

prompt: I wish you _____ make so much noise — I'm trying to concentrate.
why: 'Wish + would' for annoying habits you want to change.

prompt: If only I _____ taller! I can never reach the top shelf.
why: 'If only + were' for present/unreal wish.

prompt: She wishes she _____ a different career path.
why: 'Wish + past perfect' for regret about a past choice.

prompt: I wish I _____ (know) about the job opportunity sooner.
why: Past perfect after 'wish' for past regret.

prompt: If only the traffic _____ (not/be) so bad — we missed the first act.
why: Past perfect negative after 'if only'.

prompt: I wish he _____ (stop) interrupting me every five minutes.
why: 'Wish + would' for an annoying current habit.

prompt: She wishes she _____ (speak) better Spanish before her trip to Madrid.
why: Past perfect after 'wish' — regret about past ability.

prompt: If only I _____ (have) more confidence in job interviews.
why: 'If only + simple past' for present wish.

prompt: Express as a wish: 'I didn't study medicine. I regret it.'
answer: I wish I had studied medicine.
accept: I wish I had studied medicine.
If only I had studied medicine.
why: Regret about past = 'wish/if only + past perfect'.

prompt: Express as a wish: 'He keeps leaving the door open and it annoys me.'
answer: I wish he would stop leaving the door open.
accept: I wish he wouldn't leave the door open.
I wish he would stop leaving the door open.
why: Annoying habit = 'wish + would + change in behaviour'.

prompt: Write a sentence using 'I wish' or 'if only' to express a genuine regret about a past decision.
model_answer: If only I had taken more language classes at university — it would have opened so many more doors.

prompt: Write two connected sentences: one expressing a present wish and one explaining why.
rubric: Present wish with simple past or 'were'
Explanation uses appropriate tense or structure
model_answer: I wish I lived closer to the city centre. The daily commute takes nearly two hours, which leaves me exhausted by the time I get home.

prompt: _____ the report, she noticed several inconsistencies.
why: Present participle clause for simultaneous action.

prompt: _____ in 1889, the tower has become an iconic symbol of France.
why: Past participle clause in passive meaning.

prompt: _____ her presentation, she felt confident and relieved.
why: 'Having + pp' for an action completed before the main verb.

prompt: The package _____ on time, the client was satisfied.
why: Past participle clause with implied passive meaning.

prompt: Not _____ where to go, they stopped to ask for directions.
why: Negative present participle clause: 'Not knowing…'

prompt: _____ (overwhelm) by the response, the charity extended the campaign.
why: Passive past participle clause for an emotional state.

prompt: _____ (finish) dinner, they went for a walk along the river.
why: 'Having + pp' for prior completed action.

prompt: _____ (sit) by the window, she watched the rain fall on the street below.
why: Present participle for simultaneous action.

prompt: _____ (lose) his passport, he was unable to board the flight.
why: 'Having lost' = prior causal event.

prompt: The new regulation, _____ (introduce) last month, has already sparked controversy.
why: Past participle relative clause (defining).

prompt: Combine using a participle clause: 'She reviewed all the files. Then she wrote her report.'
answer: Having reviewed all the files, she wrote her report.
accept: Having reviewed all the files, she wrote her report.
Reviewing all the files, she then wrote her report.
why: 'Having + pp' for completed prior action.

prompt: Reduce the relative clause to a participle: 'The students who were sitting at the back couldn't hear well.'
answer: The students sitting at the back couldn't hear well.
accept: The students sitting at the back couldn't hear well.
why: Remove 'who were' → present participle.

prompt: Write a sentence with a present participle clause describing two things happening at the same time.
rubric: Subjects of both clauses are the same
model_answer: Walking through the market, she spotted a rare edition of the book she had been searching for.

prompt: Write a sentence beginning with 'Having + past participle' about something you did before starting a task.
model_answer: Having checked all the data twice, he submitted the report with confidence.

prompt: By this time next year, I _____ graduated and started my career.
why: Future perfect for a completed action before a future point.

prompt: She _____ the airport by the time you read this.
why: Future perfect for completion before a stated future time.

prompt: Look at those clouds — it _____ rain soon.
why: 'Going to' for predictions based on present evidence.

prompt: I _____ my colleague while she is in the hospital this afternoon.
why: 'Am visiting' — arranged future plan with time marker.

prompt: 'The phone is ringing!' 'I _____ answer it.'
why: 'Will' for spontaneous decisions made at the moment of speaking.

prompt: This time tomorrow, we _____ (fly) over the Atlantic.
why: Future continuous for an action in progress at a future moment.

prompt: By the end of the month, they _____ (complete) the renovation.
why: Future perfect for completion before a deadline.

prompt: The train _____ (leave) at 09:15. Don't be late.
why: Present simple for a scheduled/timetabled event.

prompt: I _____ (be about to) send the email when the server crashed.
why: 'Was about to' for an imminent past action interrupted.

prompt: They _____ (go to) open a new branch in the city centre next spring.
why: 'Going to' for a planned intention.

prompt: Rewrite to show the action will be in progress: 'I will work at 8 pm.'
answer: I will be working at 8 pm.
accept: I will be working at 8 pm.
why: Future continuous for an ongoing action at a specific future time.

prompt: Rewrite to show completion before a deadline: 'She finishes the project by Friday.'
answer: She will have finished the project by Friday.
accept: She will have finished the project by Friday.
why: Future perfect: 'will have + pp' before a future point.

prompt: Write a sentence about what you will have achieved by the end of this year using the future perfect.
rubric: References a future deadline or time expression
model_answer: By the end of this year, I will have completed my language course and taken the B2 certification exam.

prompt: Write two sentences: one using 'going to' (plan) and one using 'will' (spontaneous decision), about the same topic.
rubric: 'Going to' correctly used for a pre-made plan
'Will' correctly used for a spontaneous or on-the-spot decision
model_answer: I am going to visit my family in Barcelona next month — we booked the tickets weeks ago. Oh, the flight is delayed? I'll grab a coffee while I wait, then.

prompt: She _____ have left already — her coat is gone.
why: 'Must have' = logical deduction from present evidence.

prompt: He _____ have taken the wrong turn — he doesn't know this area well.
why: 'Might have' = possibility in the past.

prompt: They _____ have arrived by now — the journey only takes two hours.
why: 'Should have arrived' = expectation based on normal time.

prompt: She _____ have seen the email — she was copied in on it.
why: 'Can't have' = logical impossibility / strong negative deduction.

prompt: That _____ be the new manager — she matches the description perfectly.
why: 'Must' for strong present deduction from evidence.

prompt: The lights are on — they _____ (be) at home.
why: Present deduction from observable evidence.

prompt: He _____ (not/take) the shortcut — he arrived later than everyone else.
why: Negative past deduction.

prompt: She _____ (leave) her phone at the restaurant — it's not in her bag.
why: Strong positive past deduction.

prompt: They _____ (know) about the problem beforehand — they seemed so surprised.
why: Strong negative past deduction.

prompt: It _____ (rain) heavily last night — the streets are still flooded.
why: Past deduction from present evidence.

prompt: Express as a deduction: 'I'm sure she has met him before — they seem very comfortable together.'
answer: She must have met him before.
accept: She must have met him before.
why: Strong past deduction = 'must have + pp'.

prompt: Express as a negative deduction: 'It's impossible that he read the brief — he doesn't know any of the details.'
answer: He can't have read the brief.
accept: He can't have read the brief.
He couldn't have read the brief.
why: 'Can't/couldn't have + pp' for impossibility in the past.

prompt: Look around you and write two deduction sentences using different modals (e.g., must, might, can't).
rubric: Present or past deduction clearly expressed
model_answer: The office must be very busy today — I can hear phones ringing constantly. The manager might have called an emergency meeting, as I noticed several people heading to the conference room.

prompt: Write a sentence speculating about a historical mystery using 'could have', 'may have', or 'might have'.
rubric: Refers plausibly to a past scenario
model_answer: The colony may have been abandoned due to a severe drought, although historians still debate whether conflict with neighbouring tribes could have played a role.

prompt: _____ the circumstances, the board decided to postpone the vote.
why: 'In light of' = considering; multi-word preposition.

prompt: She spoke _____ all the volunteers when she accepted the award.
why: 'On behalf of' = representing.

prompt: The project was delayed _____ a shortage of materials.
why: 'Owing to' = because of; prepositional phrase of cause.

prompt: The report was positive _____ a few minor criticisms.
why: 'Apart from' = except for / other than.

prompt: The deal was structured _____ protecting both parties' interests.
why: 'With a view to + gerund' = with the intention of.

prompt: He was promoted _____ his outstanding contribution to the project.
why: Prepositional phrase of cause/reason.

prompt: They changed the policy _____ reducing staff turnover.
why: 'With a view to + gerund' expresses purpose.

prompt: The meeting was productive _____ the last agenda item, which overran.
why: 'Apart from' introduces an exception.

prompt: She is in charge of the project _____ the director's absence.
why: 'In the absence of' — fixed prepositional phrase.

prompt: The law was passed _____ strong public opposition.
why: Concessive prepositional phrase.

prompt: Replace the underlined phrase with a complex preposition: 'Because of the bad weather, the match was cancelled.'
answer: Owing to the bad weather, the match was cancelled.
accept: Owing to the bad weather, the match was cancelled.
Due to the bad weather, the match was cancelled.
On account of the bad weather, the match was cancelled.
why: Complex prepositions of cause.

prompt: Rewrite using 'with a view to': 'They redesigned the app to attract younger users.'
answer: They redesigned the app with a view to attracting younger users.
accept: They redesigned the app with a view to attracting younger users.
why: 'With a view to + gerund'.

prompt: Write a formal sentence using 'in light of', 'in view of', or 'given' to introduce a reason for a decision.
model_answer: In light of the recent data breach, the company has decided to overhaul its entire cybersecurity infrastructure.

prompt: Write a sentence using 'apart from' or 'with the exception of' to introduce an exception.
rubric: 'Apart from' or 'with the exception of' before a noun phrase
Main clause logically contrasts with the exception
model_answer: Apart from the conclusion, which needs further development, the essay is well argued and clearly structured.

prompt: Which is most appropriate in a formal email?
options: I'm writing to let you know about…
why: Formal emails use full sentences and polite indirect phrasing.

prompt: 'Could you please clarify your position on this matter?' is _____ register.
why: 'Could you please' + formal noun 'this matter' marks formal register.

prompt: Which phrase is most informal?
options: I would be grateful for your response.
Please do not hesitate to contact us.
Get back to me when you can!
We look forward to hearing from you.
why: 'Get back to me' is informal/colloquial.

prompt: 'We regret to inform you that your application has been unsuccessful.' → informal version:
options: We are sorry to tell you that you were not selected.
We wish to advise that your candidacy was not progressed.
why: 'Sorry, you didn't get it' is the most informal recast.

prompt: 'Loads of' is to 'a large number of' as 'get rid of' is to:
why: 'Eliminate' is the formal equivalent of 'get rid of'.

prompt: Formal: 'We wish to _____ (confirm) receipt of your application.'
why: Formal verb 'confirm'; informal would say 'let you know we got'.

prompt: Informal → formal: 'She blew off the meeting.' → 'She _____ the meeting.'
why: Formal avoids idiomatic 'blew off'.

prompt: 'I am writing _____ (enquire about) the vacancy advertised on your website.'
why: Formal purpose infinitive.

prompt: 'The meeting was _____ (put off).' → formal: 'The meeting was _____.'
why: 'Postponed' is the formal equivalent of 'put off'.

prompt: 'I'm really sorry about the mix-up.' → formal: 'We _____ (apologise) for any inconvenience caused.'
why: Formal apology uses full verb + adverb.

prompt: Make formal: 'Thanks a lot for getting back to me so fast!'
answer: Thank you for your prompt response.
accept: Thank you for your prompt response.
I am grateful for your swift reply.
Many thanks for responding so quickly.
why: Replace informality with formal noun phrases.

prompt: Make informal: 'We would be most grateful if you could provide your feedback at your earliest convenience.'
answer: Let us know what you think when you get a chance.
accept: Let us know what you think when you get a chance.
Please give us your feedback when you can.
Can you give us some feedback soon?
why: Replace modal + noun phrase with simpler verb phrases.

prompt: Write the opening sentence of a formal letter requesting information about a course or service.
model_answer: I am writing to enquire about the advanced language courses offered at your institution and to request a prospectus for the upcoming academic year.

prompt: Rewrite this informal message in formal register: 'Hey, just wondering if the report is done? We kind of need it ASAP.'
rubric: Formal salutation or direct professional opening
model_answer: I am writing to kindly request an update on the progress of the report, as we require it as soon as possible in order to meet our deadline.

prompt: _____ the students passed the exam — only three failed.
why: 'The majority of' is correct before 'the + noun'; 'most of' also works; 'the most of' is wrong.

prompt: There is _____ evidence to support this claim.
why: 'Little' (no article) = not much, with uncountable nouns.

prompt: _____ what she said made sense to me.
why: 'None of + what she said' — pronoun reference.

prompt: He has _____ experience in project management.
why: 'A great deal of' for uncountable nouns.

prompt: _____ solutions were proposed, but none were viable.
why: 'Several' with countable plural.

prompt: Very _____ (few/little) progress was made in the first round of talks.
why: 'Progress' is uncountable → 'little'.

prompt: _____ (few/little) of the candidates met the minimum requirements.
why: 'Candidates' is countable → 'few'.

prompt: She has spent _____ (a great deal of/a large number of) money on equipment.
why: 'Money' is uncountable.

prompt: _____ (neither/none) of the three proposals was accepted.
why: 'None of' for three or more items.

prompt: The survey revealed that _____ (the majority/most) respondents favoured remote working.
why: Both are correct; 'the majority of' is more formal.

prompt: Correct: 'She has very few informations about the case.'
answer: She has very little information about the case.
accept: She has very little information about the case.
why: 'Information' is uncountable: 'little', not 'few'; no plural 's'.

prompt: Correct: 'Most of students failed the test.'
answer: Most of the students failed the test.
accept: Most of the students failed the test.
why: 'Most of' requires a determiner before the noun: 'most of the'; or use 'most students' without 'of'.

prompt: Write a sentence using 'a considerable amount of' or 'a significant number of' in a formal context.
model_answer: A considerable amount of time was spent reviewing the terms of the contract before both parties reached an agreement.

prompt: Write a sentence contrasting two quantifiers ('few'/'little' vs 'a few'/'a little') to show a difference in meaning.
rubric: Meaning distinction is clear (negative vs positive implication)
model_answer: Few students volunteered to present, which disappointed the teacher; however, a few of them agreed to help organise the event instead.

prompt: 'Did you finish the report?' 'I tried _____.''
why: 'Tried to' — infinitive ellipsis: 'to' replaces 'to finish the report'.

prompt: She said she would help, and _____ she did.
why: 'And so she did' — substitution with 'so' for a previous verb phrase.

prompt: 'Are you coming to the party?' 'I hope _____.''
why: 'I hope so' — 'so' substitutes for a positive clause.

prompt: 'Has she called back?' 'I don't think _____.''
why: 'I don't think so' — negative substitution with 'so'.

prompt: 'Should I apply?' 'If you want _____.''
why: 'If you want to' — infinitive ellipsis after 'want'.

prompt: 'Will the train be on time?' 'It should _____.''
why: After a modal in ellipsis, the bare infinitive is retained: 'It should be' (on time).

prompt: He promised to call, and _____ he did — at exactly midnight.
why: 'So he did' for affirmative confirmation.

prompt: 'Do you want coffee or tea?' 'Either _____ fine.'
why: 'Either is fine' — substitution; no verb ellipsis here but subject substitution.

prompt: 'Can you finish by tomorrow?' 'I'll try _____.''
why: 'Try to' — infinitive ellipsis.

prompt: She said the project was behind schedule, and it _____ (be).
why: 'And it was' — auxiliary substitution for the state.

prompt: Reduce using ellipsis: 'He wanted to apply for the job but he decided not to apply for the job.'
answer: He wanted to apply for the job but decided not to.
accept: He wanted to apply for the job but decided not to.
why: Remove repeated infinitive phrase after 'not to'.

prompt: Add 'so do I' or 'neither do I' as a tag: 'I enjoy long walks in nature.'
answer: I enjoy long walks in nature. So do I.
why: 'So do I' for agreeing with a positive statement.

prompt: Write a short exchange (2 lines) using ellipsis: one question and one short answer using 'to', 'so', or an auxiliary only.
rubric: Ellipsis clearly replaces a repeated element
The short answer is grammatically correct
model_answer: 'Are you planning to attend the conference?' 'I hope to, yes — it depends on my schedule.'

prompt: Write two sentences where you use 'so' as a clause substitute (e.g., 'I think so', 'I believe so').
rubric: 'So' substitutes for a full clause in both sentences
model_answer: I think so — the latest figures certainly point in that direction. I believe so too, though we should wait for the official announcement before drawing any conclusions.

prompt: The factory was closed _____ safety violations.
why: 'Due to' + noun phrase for cause.

prompt: He spoke quietly _____ not to disturb the other passengers.
why: 'So as not to + infinitive' = purpose with negative.

prompt: The team worked overtime _____ meet the deadline.
why: 'In order to + infinitive' = purpose.

prompt: Traffic congestion was so severe _____ the event had to be rescheduled.
why: 'So + adjective + that' = result clause.

prompt: She saved money _____ could buy a new laptop.
why: 'So that + subject + modal' for purpose with different subjects.

prompt: He turned down the volume _____ (so as / so that) not to wake the baby.
why: 'So as not to + infinitive' for negative purpose.

prompt: The flight was delayed _____ (due to / because) adverse weather conditions.
why: 'Due to' + noun phrase.

prompt: They launched an early marketing campaign _____ (so that / in order to) build awareness before the product release.
why: 'In order to' + infinitive for purpose with same subject.

prompt: It was such a complex issue _____ no single solution could address it.
why: 'Such + noun phrase + that' = result.

prompt: The temperature dropped so sharply _____ crops were destroyed overnight.
why: 'So + adverb + that' = result.

prompt: Combine using 'in order to': 'She practised every day. She wanted to improve her pronunciation.'
answer: She practised every day in order to improve her pronunciation.
accept: She practised every day in order to improve her pronunciation.
In order to improve her pronunciation, she practised every day.
why: 'In order to' links action to its purpose.

prompt: Rewrite using 'so…that': 'The exam was very difficult. Nobody passed it.'
answer: The exam was so difficult that nobody passed it.
accept: The exam was so difficult that nobody passed it.
why: 'So + adjective + that' for result.

prompt: Write a sentence about a decision you made, using 'so that' or 'in order to' to express your purpose.
model_answer: I started learning Spanish so that I could communicate with my colleagues in the Madrid office without relying on a translator.

prompt: Write a cause-and-effect sentence about an environmental issue using 'as a result' or 'consequently'.
model_answer: Carbon emissions have continued to rise sharply over the past decade. As a result, global temperatures have reached record highs, threatening ecosystems worldwide.

prompt: The city needs to _____ measures to tackle air pollution.
why: 'Take measures' is the fixed collocation.

prompt: She _____ a proposal to extend the project deadline.
why: 'Make a proposal' is the correct collocation.

prompt: The committee will _____ a decision by the end of the week.
why: 'Reach a decision' (consensus meaning); 'make a decision' is also correct but 'reach' fits committee/group context.

prompt: They _____ a deal after two weeks of negotiations.
why: 'Make a deal' or 'strike a deal' are standard; 'reach' also valid.

prompt: The new law will _____ an impact on small businesses.
why: 'Have an impact' is the correct collocation.

prompt: The government plans to _____ (take/make) steps to improve public transport.
why: 'Take steps' — fixed collocation.

prompt: She _____ (do/make) a mistake by ignoring the early warning signs.
why: 'Make a mistake' — standard collocation.

prompt: He _____ (have/make) difficulty understanding the instructions.
why: 'Have difficulty' — standard collocation with uncountable noun.

prompt: The team _____ (reach/make) a consensus after a long discussion.
why: 'Reach a consensus' — group decision collocation.

prompt: She _____ (give/make) a speech at the annual conference.
why: 'Give/deliver a speech' — both are standard collocations.

prompt: Correct the collocation: 'They did a great effort to finish on time.'
answer: They made a great effort to finish on time.
accept: They made a great effort to finish on time.
why: 'Make an effort' — not 'do an effort'.

prompt: Correct the collocation: 'We need to make progress on this issue.'
answer: We need to make progress on this issue.
accept: We need to make progress on this issue.
why: 'Make progress' is correct — this sentence is already correct; the focus is recognising valid collocations.

prompt: Write a sentence using two of these collocations: make/take/reach a decision, have an impact, take action.
model_answer: The committee needs to reach a decision soon, as further delays will have a significant impact on the project timeline.

prompt: Write a professional sentence using 'raise awareness', 'address a problem', or 'meet a deadline'.
model_answer: The campaign successfully raised awareness about the importance of mental health in the workplace, prompting the company to address the problem of employee burnout more directly.

prompt: 'The merger fell through' means the merger:
why: 'Fall through' = to fail / not happen.

prompt: 'The company brought in a consultant' — formal equivalent:
why: 'Bring in' = hire/employ.

prompt: 'The project was called off.' — formal verb:
why: 'Call off' = cancel.

prompt: 'She put forward a new idea.' — formal equivalent:
why: 'Put forward' = propose / present.

prompt: 'The prices went up sharply.' — formal:
why: 'Go up' = increase; 'rose' and 'increased' are both formal, 'increased' is the most neutral formal choice.

prompt: Formal: 'The board _____ (bring forward) the proposal for a merger.' → 'The board _____ the proposal.'
why: 'Put forward' or 'propose/table' in formal contexts.

prompt: 'Sales _____ (go up) by 15% in the second quarter.' → formal: 'Sales _____ by 15%.'
why: Formal single-word verbs replace 'go up'.

prompt: 'The deal _____ (fall apart) due to legal complications.' → 'The deal _____ due to legal complications.'
why: 'Fall apart/through' → 'collapse/fail' in formal register.

prompt: 'The manager _____ (put off) the meeting until Thursday.' → formal: 'The manager _____ the meeting.'
why: 'Put off' → 'postpone/defer'.

prompt: 'They _____ (come up with) a solution to the supply crisis.' → formal: 'They _____ a solution.'
why: 'Come up with' → 'devise/develop/identify'.

prompt: Replace the phrasal verb with a formal single word: 'The talks broke down after only one session.'
answer: The talks collapsed after only one session.
accept: The talks collapsed after only one session.
The talks failed after only one session.
The talks ended in deadlock after only one session.
why: 'Break down' → 'collapse/fail' in formal writing.

prompt: Replace the phrasal verb: 'The committee looked into the allegations.'
why: 'Look into' → 'investigate/examine'.

prompt: Write a formal sentence about a business or academic situation using the formal equivalent of 'find out', 'give up', or 'set up'.
rubric: Formal single-word verb used (discover/ascertain; abandon; establish/create)
model_answer: The research team was able to ascertain the root cause of the failure through a series of controlled experiments.

prompt: Rewrite in formal register: 'The company put off launching the product because things fell through with their main supplier.'
rubric: Both phrasal verbs replaced with formal equivalents
model_answer: The company postponed the product launch after negotiations with their primary supplier collapsed.

prompt: She is very enthusiastic _____ the new project.
why: 'Enthusiastic about' is the fixed collocation.

prompt: There has been a significant increase _____ unemployment rates.
why: 'Increase in' — preposition after noun indicating a change in a field.

prompt: He is responsible _____ overseeing the entire operation.
why: 'Responsible for' — fixed adjective + preposition.

prompt: The report is based _____ data collected over three years.
why: 'Based on' — fixed collocation.

prompt: She has a talent _____ languages.
why: 'A talent for' — noun + preposition.

prompt: He is aware _____ the risks involved in the procedure.
why: 'Aware of' — adjective + preposition.

prompt: The decline _____ biodiversity is a major environmental concern.
why: 'Decline in' — used for quantities/levels.

prompt: They are committed _____ reducing carbon emissions by 2030.
why: 'Committed to + gerund' — adjective + preposition.

prompt: There is a strong demand _____ affordable housing in urban areas.
why: 'Demand for' — noun + preposition.

prompt: She is proud _____ her team's achievements.
why: 'Proud of' — fixed adjective + preposition.

prompt: Correct: 'He has a strong belief on the power of education.'
answer: He has a strong belief in the power of education.
accept: He has a strong belief in the power of education.
why: 'Belief in' — not 'belief on'.

prompt: Correct: 'She is very good in solving problems under pressure.'
answer: She is very good at solving problems under pressure.
accept: She is very good at solving problems under pressure.
why: 'Good at' — not 'good in'.

prompt: Write a sentence using two adjective + preposition collocations (e.g., 'aware of', 'responsible for', 'capable of').
model_answer: She is aware of the challenges ahead and feels capable of handling them without additional support.

prompt: Write a sentence using a noun + preposition collocation (e.g., 'rise in', 'lack of', 'solution to', 'approach to').
model_answer: The lack of investment in public infrastructure has contributed to the steady decline in service quality across the region.

prompt: Which is the best thesis statement for a discursive essay?
options: In this essay I will talk about renewable energy.
Renewable energy offers a viable path to a sustainable future, though significant investment and policy reform are required.
I think renewable energy is good.
Renewable energy is very important today.
why: A good thesis is specific, debatable, and previews the argument.

prompt: Which sentence best introduces a counterargument in a formal essay?
options: Those who oppose this view argue that…
On the other side of the argument, opponents claim that…
why: Formal register + full clause + appropriate concessive marker.

prompt: 'In conclusion' should be followed by:
options: a summary of main points and a final position
why: Conclusions summarise and close; new arguments belong in body paragraphs.

prompt: 'Moreover' is used to:
why: 'Moreover' = furthermore / in addition.

prompt: Which body paragraph opening is most effective?
options: One significant advantage of this approach is that it reduces costs while maintaining quality.
why: Topic sentence that is specific, evaluative, and links to the thesis.

prompt: _____ (to give an example), studies have shown that exercise can reduce symptoms of depression by up to 30%.
why: Discourse marker introducing evidence or example.

prompt: The policy has reduced crime rates. _____, it has improved community relations.
why: Addition marker for a further supporting point.

prompt: _____ the evidence is compelling, the cost of implementation remains a serious obstacle.
why: Concessive subordinator to acknowledge a point before a counter.

prompt: _____ (to conclude), the benefits of the policy clearly outweigh the drawbacks.
why: Standard concluding marker.

prompt: The data _____ (suggest) a strong correlation between education levels and economic mobility.
why: Formal present simple or hedged form for reporting data.

prompt: Improve this opening: 'In this essay I will write about why climate change is bad.'
answer: This essay examines the principal causes of climate change and considers the most effective policy responses.
accept: This essay examines the principal causes of climate change and considers the most effective policy responses.
This essay argues that immediate action on climate change is essential to prevent irreversible environmental damage.
why: Remove 'I will write about'; use more formal, specific framing.

prompt: Add a counterargument concession: 'Some argue that immigration puts pressure on public services.'
answer: While some argue that immigration puts pressure on public services, the evidence suggests that migrants contribute significantly more to the economy than they consume.
accept: While some argue that immigration puts pressure on public services, the evidence suggests that migrants contribute significantly more to the economy than they consume.
Some argue that immigration puts pressure on public services; however, research indicates that this view oversimplifies a complex issue.
why: Acknowledge + rebut with 'while/however'.

prompt: Write a topic sentence for a body paragraph arguing that technology improves education.
rubric: Links to a wider thesis about education or technology
model_answer: Technology has transformed educational access by enabling students in remote areas to attend high-quality virtual classes, thereby reducing geographical inequality in learning outcomes.

prompt: Write a concluding sentence that restates the thesis without repeating it word for word.
model_answer: Ultimately, the evidence demonstrates that a balanced approach — combining technological innovation with robust regulatory frameworks — offers the most sustainable path to addressing the challenges of modern urban development.

prompt: The _____ of the plan was praised by all stakeholders.
why: Noun form after 'the': 'efficiency'.

prompt: She gave a very _____ presentation at the conference.
why: Adjective modifying 'presentation': 'persuasive'.

prompt: The decision was made _____, without consulting the team.
why: Adverb modifying a verb: 'unilaterally'.

prompt: There is growing _____ about the long-term effects of social media.
why: Uncountable noun after 'growing': 'concern'.

prompt: The company showed great _____ in handling the crisis.
why: Abstract noun: 'resilience'.

prompt: His _____ (refuse) to compromise led to the breakdown of talks.
why: Noun form of 'refuse': 'refusal'.

prompt: The results were _____ (signify) higher than predicted.
why: Adverb modifying 'higher'.

prompt: Her _____ (dedicate) to the project inspired the whole team.
why: Noun form of 'dedicate'.

prompt: The new regulations are intended to _____ (simple) the application process.
why: Verb form: 'simplify'.

prompt: The _____ (innovate) of the design won several awards.
why: Noun form of 'innovate'.

prompt: Change to the correct form: 'The company was criticise for its lack of transparent.'
answer: The company was criticised for its lack of transparency.
accept: The company was criticised for its lack of transparency.
why: 'Criticised' (passive) and 'transparency' (noun form).

prompt: Change to the correct form: 'She spoke very convince at the conference.'
answer: She spoke very convincingly at the conference.
accept: She spoke very convincingly at the conference.
why: Adverb 'convincingly' to modify the verb 'spoke'.

prompt: Write a sentence using the noun, adjective, and adverb forms of 'innovate' in a single sentence or two connected sentences.
model_answer: The company's latest innovation is truly innovative, and it was launched so innovatively that it quickly dominated the market.

prompt: Write a sentence using the correct word form of TWO of these roots: persist, analyse, collaborate, accurate.
rubric: Forms chosen match the grammatical context
model_answer: Her persistence in conducting a thorough analysis of the data earned her the respect of her colleagues.

prompt: 'The project is on thin ice' means it is:
why: 'On thin ice' = in a precarious or risky situation.

prompt: 'She hit the nail on the head' means she:
options: identified the exact problem or solution
why: 'Hit the nail on the head' = said something exactly right.

prompt: 'They burned their bridges' means they:
why: 'Burn bridges' = destroy relationships making return impossible.

prompt: 'The deal fell through at the eleventh hour' means:
options: it failed at the last moment
why: 'At the eleventh hour' = at the last possible moment; 'fell through' = failed.

prompt: 'She kept the team in the loop' means she:
why: 'Keep in the loop' = keep someone regularly updated.

prompt: After months of negotiations, they finally _____ (reach/break) the ice and began to make progress.
why: 'Break the ice' = initiate contact or ease tension.

prompt: Don't _____ (jump/run) to conclusions before we have all the facts.
why: 'Jump to conclusions' = decide too quickly without evidence.

prompt: The new policy is just a _____ (quick/band) fix that doesn't address the root cause.
why: 'Band-aid fix' = a temporary or superficial solution.

prompt: She managed to _____ (bite/chew) off more than she could chew by taking on three projects at once.
why: 'Bite off more than you can chew' = take on too much.

prompt: Let's not _____ (put/place) all our eggs in one basket — we should pursue several options.
why: 'Put all eggs in one basket' = rely on a single option.

prompt: Explain in plain language: 'We're back to square one with the negotiations.'
answer: We have to start the negotiations again from the beginning because no progress was made.
accept: We have to start the negotiations again from the beginning because no progress was made.
The negotiations have failed and we must start over.
why: 'Back to square one' = starting over from the beginning.

prompt: Replace with an appropriate idiom: 'The manager told us all the private information about the company's difficulties.'
answer: The manager spilled the beans about the company's difficulties.
accept: The manager spilled the beans about the company's difficulties.
The manager let the cat out of the bag about the company's difficulties.
why: 'Spill the beans' = reveal confidential information.

prompt: Write a sentence using one of these idioms correctly in a professional or academic context: 'the tip of the iceberg', 'cut corners', 'go back to the drawing board'.
model_answer: The recent data breach is merely the tip of the iceberg — a full audit revealed systemic security failures throughout the organisation.

prompt: Write a short anecdote (2-3 sentences) naturally incorporating two different idioms.
model_answer: When our initial launch plan fell apart, we went back to the drawing board and redesigned the entire campaign from scratch. It was hard work, but in the end our persistence paid off and the product exceeded our sales targets.

prompt: Which word is spelt correctly?
why: 'Accommodation' has double 'c' and double 'm'.

prompt: Which word contains a silent letter?
why: 'triumph' (silent 'ph' = f, but 'p' is not silent here); 'knight' (silent 'k'); 'receipt' (silent 'p') — 'all of the above' is incorrect for triumph, so best answer is 'all of the above' only if triumph has a silent letter. Actually 'triumph' has no silent letter. Correct: 'receipt' (silent p) and 'knight' (silent k).

prompt: Which pair are homophones?
why: 'Stationary' (not moving) and 'stationery' (paper/pens) are homophones.

prompt: 'Necessary' is often misspelt. The correct spelling has:
why: N-E-C-E-S-S-A-R-Y: one 'c', two 's'.

prompt: Which word is the correct British English spelling?
why: British English prefers '-ise' but 'analyse' always ends in '-yse' in BrE. 'Realize', 'memorize', 'criticize' → British preference is '-ise' but '-ize' is also accepted by some style guides; 'analyse' is unambiguously BrE.

prompt: The meeting was _____ (postpone / postponed) due to the CEO's sudden illness.
why: Passive requires past participle.

prompt: Please ensure your _____ (correspondence / correspondance) is sent before the deadline.
why: Correct spelling: 'correspondence'.

prompt: The _____ (occurrence / occurence) of such errors is unacceptable.
why: 'Occurrence' has double 'c' and double 'r'.

prompt: The committee _____ (recommend / recomend) increasing the budget.
why: 'Recommend' has double 'm'.

prompt: Her _____ (achievement / acheivement) in the field was remarkable.
why: 'i before e' rule: 'achieve' → 'achievement'.

prompt: Correct the spelling errors: 'The goverment anounced a new enviromental policy.'
answer: The government announced a new environmental policy.
accept: The government announced a new environmental policy.
why: 'government' (no missing letter); 'announced' (double n); 'environmental'.

prompt: Correct the spelling: 'She recieved an unecessary warning from her supervisor.'
answer: She received an unnecessary warning from her supervisor.
accept: She received an unnecessary warning from her supervisor.
why: 'received' (ei after c); 'unnecessary' (double n, one c, double s).

prompt: Write a sentence containing at least three commonly misspelt words (e.g., necessary, accommodation, committee, occurrence, separate) — all correctly spelt.
model_answer: The committee agreed that the accommodation provided was necessary, but raised concerns about the occurrence of maintenance issues.

prompt: Write a sentence using the correct homophone in each pair: 'affect/effect', 'complement/compliment', 'principal/principle'.
rubric: Meaning of each is clear in context
model_answer: The new lighting will complement the decor and could have a positive effect on staff wellbeing — a principle the principal has supported from the start.

prompt: When a writer says 'the policy has had mixed results', they imply:
options: some outcomes were positive and some negative
why: 'Mixed results' = both positive and negative outcomes.

prompt: 'It remains to be seen whether the investment will pay off' suggests:
options: the writer is confident it will succeed
the writer disapproves of the investment
why: 'Remains to be seen' = the outcome is not yet known.

prompt: A text says 'critics were less than enthusiastic'. This means critics were:
why: 'Less than enthusiastic' is an understatement meaning disappointed or negative.

prompt: 'The minister stopped short of calling it a failure.' This implies:
options: the minister said it was a complete failure
the minister came close to calling it a failure but didn't
the minister denied it was a failure
why: 'Stop short of' = nearly do something but not quite.

prompt: 'The proposal attracted considerable attention' most likely means:
options: many people were interested or concerned
why: 'Attracted considerable attention' = many people noticed / were interested.

prompt: 'The author _____ (imply/infer) that the character is hiding something.' — the author's action is to _____.
why: Authors 'imply'; readers 'infer'.

prompt: 'He read between the _____ (lines/words) and realised the email was a warning.'
why: 'Read between the lines' = understand hidden meaning.

prompt: The phrase 'it is worth noting that' signals the writer is about to make an _____ (important/optional) point.
why: 'It is worth noting that' flags an important detail.

prompt: 'The report glosses over several key issues.' This suggests the report _____ (addresses/avoids) them superficially.
why: 'Gloss over' = deal with something briefly and inadequately.

prompt: 'Not without controversy' means the subject _____ (was / was not) debated.
why: Double negative: 'not without controversy' = it was controversial.

prompt: Paraphrase: 'The results left much to be desired.'
answer: The results were disappointing / not as good as expected.
accept: The results were not as good as expected.
why: 'Leave much to be desired' = be unsatisfactory.

prompt: Identify the implied meaning: 'The committee was not exactly overjoyed at the news.'
answer: The committee was disappointed or unhappy about the news.
accept: The committee was disappointed or unhappy about the news.
why: 'Not exactly overjoyed' = understatement for disappointment.

prompt: Write a sentence that implies something negative without stating it directly, using understatement.
rubric: Negative meaning implied, not stated outright
Understatement device used (e.g., 'not exactly', 'less than', 'left much to be desired')
model_answer: The new website redesign was, shall we say, not exactly greeted with universal enthusiasm by the user community.

prompt: Write a short sentence (or two) where the reader must infer the speaker's attitude from word choice alone.
model_answer: The presentation lasted nearly three hours and covered topics already addressed in last week's briefing. By the time the final slide appeared, most attendees had found reasons to check their phones.

prompt: Which is an appropriate heading for a section of a formal report?
why: Report headings are numbered, formal, and descriptive.

prompt: A proposal differs from a report in that a proposal primarily:
why: Proposals argue for and recommend a course of action.

prompt: Which verb is most appropriate in the recommendations section of a report?
why: Formal impersonal 'It is recommended that' suits report register.

prompt: 'The aim of this report is to…' is:
why: Purpose statements introduce what the report sets out to do.

prompt: In a formal report, data should be presented:
options: in an organised, impersonal way using passive or impersonal structures
as bullet points only, no prose
why: Formal reports use impersonal, organised prose or structured data.

prompt: This report _____ (aim) to assess the feasibility of introducing a four-day working week.
why: Present simple in formal purpose statement.

prompt: The survey _____ (reveal) that 78% of employees would welcome flexible hours.
why: Past simple or present simple for reporting results.

prompt: It is _____ (strong) recommended that the company invest in staff training.
why: Adverb 'strongly' before 'recommended'.

prompt: The main _____ (find) of the report are summarised below.
why: 'Findings' = plural noun for research results.

prompt: In _____ (conclude), the proposed changes would benefit both staff and management.
why: 'In conclusion' — standard closing phrase.

prompt: Improve this recommendation: 'I think they should fix the car park.'
answer: It is recommended that the car park facilities be improved as a matter of priority.
accept: It is recommended that the car park facilities be improved as a matter of priority.
The report recommends that improvements be made to the car park facilities.
why: Impersonal passive + mandative subjunctive for formal recommendation.

prompt: Improve this finding sentence: 'Most people we asked said they weren't happy with the canteen.'
answer: The majority of respondents expressed dissatisfaction with the canteen facilities.
accept: The majority of respondents expressed dissatisfaction with the canteen facilities.
Survey results indicated that most participants were dissatisfied with the canteen.
why: Formal nominalisation + impersonal reporting.

prompt: Write a formal purpose statement (one sentence) for a report on the impact of remote working on employee productivity.
rubric: Impersonal opening ('This report aims to…' / 'The purpose of this report is to…')
model_answer: This report aims to examine the impact of remote working on employee productivity and to identify measures that could be introduced to optimise performance in a hybrid working environment.

prompt: Write one formal recommendation (one or two sentences) arising from a fictional survey showing that staff morale is low.
rubric: Uses formal recommendation language ('It is recommended that…' / 'The report recommends that…')
model_answer: It is recommended that management introduce a regular employee feedback programme and review current workload distribution, as the survey findings indicate that excessive pressure is the primary cause of low morale.
